articles.text: The planning permit counter. New Planning & Building permit fees will go into effect on January 1 in Piedmont. The adjustments are designed to better align each permit’s fee structure with the true cost of processing the permit. Most permit fees will increase to reflect the actual staff time spent on the permit. In some cases, fees will decrease. A complete list of new fees is available on the City’s website at piedmont.ca.gov/permits. Key changes • New and expanded categories: New permit types have been added to reflect recent changes in State law. Certain existing fees, such as solar permits, will be expanded into separate categories for residential and commercial projects. • Added valuation tiers: The new fee schedule adds two new valuation tiers for very large construction projects ($10 million and $25 million), scaling fees proportionally with the complexity of review. • Flat-fee conversions: Many common building permits (such as water heaters, HVAC systems, and EV chargers) will be converted from valuation-based to flat Photo courtesy of the city fees, making costs more predictable and aligned with the service provided. The goal is not to raise revenue, but to ensure each permit type is charged fairly and in proportion to the staff time and resources required to process it. The fee updates were adopted by City Council in September, following a comprehensive study. Considered a best practice in municipal operations, fee studies compare the cost of providing services to the fees charged to ensure they are fair, transparent, and based on data. Piedmont’s fee study found that the fees were only recovering 73% of the cost of permit services, resulting in a loss of revenue of more than $400,000 per year. The fee study was initiated by the City Council during the FY24-25 budget process, along with an organizational assessment. Together, these reviews aim to strengthen the Planning & Building Department’s capacity to provide timely, high-quality service to the community. The fee updates are the next step in aligning operations with best practices, ensuring services are delivered efficiently, equitably, and sustainably.
articles.title: New Planning & Building permit fees take effect Jan. 1

articles.text: The City of Piedmont has completed its storm drain improvement project. The city has upgraded the drainage infrastructure at eight locations and is in the process of repairing or replacing 20 sewer or storm drain maintenance holes (“manholes”). The total budget for the project is $632,008, funded from the City’s Facilities Capital Fund. Storm drain improvements consist of replacing drainage inlets, replacing outdated grates, and, in some cases, upsizing sections of storm drain pipe at problem areas throughout Piedmont. Each location prioritized for upgrades is considered a “hotspot” that routinely experiences flooding during storm events. These locations previously required ongoing monitoring and maintenance from Public Works crews. According to Piedmont’s communications manager, Echa Schneider, there are three main reasons for these upgrades. “First, some of these inlets have always been undersized – New Inlet on St James Trenching for new pipe at Sharon Avenue they were inadequate for their location even when they were first installed. Second, in some locations, infrastructure has simply deteriorated over time. Finally, infrastructure that was previously adequate is no longer sufficient as we experience more intense storms, more often due to climate change,” Schneider said. During the upsizing process of the inlets, Piedmont has decided to oversize these inlets to include a detention area to hold excess water and properly deal with peak storm conditions. “Providing that extra holding capacity is an efficient way to adapt our infrastructure to accommodate these more intense storms – allowing us to get water underground and prevent flooding during peak flow,” said Schneider. For the manhole repairs, these are being performed at locations Photos courtesy of the City where the city has identified groundwater leaking into the sanitary sewer system during storms. Where the city can do so economically, they’re replacing the maintenance hole. Where replacement is not economical, the city will rehabilitate them with a new lining. In both cases, the goal is to make them watertight. All storm drain upgrades have been completed. There are a few maintenance holes repairs left to do. The city says it should be wrapped up within the next couple of weeks. New Planning & Building permit fees will go into effect on January 1 in Piedmont. The adjustments are designed to better align each permit’s fee structure with the true cost of processing the permit. Most permit fees will increase to reflect the actual staff time spent on the permit. In some cases, fees will decrease. A complete list of new fees is available on the City’s website at piedmont.ca.gov/permits. Key changes • New and expanded categories: New permit types have been added to reflect recent changes in State law. Certain existing fees, such as solar permits, will be expanded into separate categories for residential and commercial projects. • Added valuation tiers: The new fee schedule adds two new valuation tiers for very large construction projects ($10 million and $25 million), scaling fees proportionally with the complexity of review. • Flat-fee conversions: Many common building permits (such as water heaters, HVAC systems, and EV chargers) will be converted from valuation-based to flat Photo courtesy of the city fees, making costs more predictable and aligned with the service provided. The goal is not to raise revenue, but to ensure each permit type is charged fairly and in proportion to the staff time and resources required to process it. The fee updates were adopted by City Council in September, following a comprehensive study. Considered a best practice in municipal operations, fee studies compare the cost of providing services to the fees charged to ensure they are fair, transparent, and based on data. Piedmont’s fee study found that the fees were only recovering 73% of the cost of permit services, resulting in a loss of revenue of more than $400,000 per year. The fee study was initiated by the City Council during the FY24-25 budget process, along with an organizational assessment. Together, these reviews aim to strengthen the Planning & Building Department’s capacity to provide timely, high-quality service to the community. The fee updates are the next step in aligning operations with best practices, ensuring services are delivered efficiently, equitably, and sustainably. articles.text: Piedmont resident and former syndicated journalist William Gee Wong has won a PEN America Literary Award for his memoir Sons of Chinatown. PEN awards promote writers of all cultural and racial backgrounds and educate the public and media about the nature of multicultural work. The winners will be recognized at the 36th annual PEN Oakland award event on Saturday, December 6, from 2-5 p.m. at the Black Repertory Group Theater. Wong said he was honored to receive the award, “I was very pleased to get the award because at least PEN Oakland and Ishmael recognize the value of the story that I’m telling,“ he said. Sons of Chinatown is a memoir about the impact of the Chinese Exclusion Act on one immigrant family that connects China to America through Oakland’s Chinatown. The book discusses the relationship and differences in the lives of Wong and his father. Wong first thought of writing the book in 2011 during a New Year’s party hosted at his residence. “2012, would be the centennial of my father’s arrival from China to America. I wanted to tell my father’s story to my family, because we are four generations now in America, and many of the younger people in our family don’t know his story,” Wong said. Wong spent 13 years researching and writing his memoir and eventually having it published it in 2024. “It was a search for who my father was and a search for who I am,” Wong said. Sons of Chinatown carries themes of identity and the pursuit of the American dream – how his father immigrated to America during the Chinese exclusion era of America, and how he found a home in Oakland’s Chinatown. Wong grew up trying to discover who he was as a first-generation Sons of Chinatown bookxover American. “Sons of Chinatown is really almost a testimonial to the good America. And by good America, I mean the America that welcomes immigrants from all over the world, that gives us, the descendants, many opportunities to try to achieve the American dream,” Wong said. articles.text: The Piedmont School Board recently added a Modern World History Honors course for sophomores, another weighted class in the growing list of courses available to PHS students next year. Like many high-performing Bay Area communities, PHS students increasingly feel pressure to take harder classes earlier, leaving them tracked into pathways long before they understand their interests. Early honors tracks push PHS toward narrow college prep, locking students into rigid pathways instead of fostering curiosity and exploration. Moder n World Histor y teacher Hayley Adams recalled first hearing about the proposal for the honors course from an email survey sent to students. She explained that she “had no idea” the course was being considered until she stumbled upon the notice and shared it with colleagues. Adams and fellow teacher Melanie McCauley designed the class using the strengths of the existing College Prep course and resources Adams had already developed. Although proud of the final curriculum, Adams said she is “saddened that sophomores will now be split up even more… in a kind of tracked system,” which she believes undermines diverse peer groups and shared learning experiences. Academic tracking separates students into standard, honors, or AP classes early, and those choices shape nearly everything they take later. Honors students are expected to continue on advanced paths, while others struggle to catch up, leading over time to different teachers, peers, and academic identities all based on a decision made at fourteen. The board had initially planned to adopt AP World History, which many felt would increase pressure, but Adams and McCauley’s month-long effort to create the honors alternative stopped that proposal. Unlike AP World History, which spans nearly twice the time period and focuses on a high-stakes exam, the honors class covers 1500 to the present with more flexibility and depth, emphasizing analytical reading, historiographical writing, interdisciplinary projects, activities like Model UN, and Harkness-style discussions. The history department works with English to align themes and texts across subjects. As English teacher Beth Black explained, Harkness discussions let students “pull from English texts, real world events, and historical perspectives” to deepen learning. She added that the method “takes time and dedication… to use effectively” and creates a “very intense history class” experienced only by honors students, widening the gap between sophomores. While many see the course as a valuable opportunity for students who want more challenge, others worry about its effect on school culture. AP U.S. History teacher David Keller noted that Modern World History does not fully prepare students for the junior weighted history class, but adding honors could push tracking even earlier, raising the question of how students will ever be adequately prepared. He asked, “How will 10th grade students get prepared for Honors Modern World History? The answer seems to be to make an honors ninth grade history class, which will necessitate an eighth grade class…” He also cautioned that APUSH could become more difficult for students who skip honors in sophomore year, as teachers may assume they already possess skills taught in the honors course. Student experiences with the current Modern World History class vary, but many seniors who took the standard course feel it prepared them well without the added pressure of a weighted grade. Senior Quincy Antaya explained that a weighted class might have shifted her focus toward grades instead of analytical thinking. Donovan Sar-Garza felt the current course already teaches essential skills. “The school doesn’t do a great job between the jump between freshman year and sophomore year” said sophomore Diego Branneria. Meanwhile, students like Lucia Dorsey, who enjoy history, welcomed the idea of greater depth. Even supporters of an honors option recognize its cultural impact. As weighted classes expand into 10th and potentially 9th grade, taking them can feel less like a choice and more like an unspoken requirement. At PHS, this academic arms race pressures students to “keep up” rather than explore interests or form new relationships. Sophomores, still adjusting to high school, may take on heavier loads, increasing stress and reducing community. The more students are divided into rigid pathways, the harder it is to meet new peers, discover unexpected interests, or experience high school beyond competition. Now that Honors Modern World History is permanent, the challenge is to ensure that it does not deepen segmentation or narrow students’ experiences. The school must prioritize balance: rigor without needless acceleration, opportunity without stratification, and learning that preserves shared experiences. In light of upcoming course registration, students should remember to choose classes not just for weighted GPA or perceived college advantage, but for genuine interest and growth. Colleges care less about how many advanced courses you take and more about how those classes have shaped your thinking, curiosity, and character. Evolette Mak is a senior at Piedmont High School and an intern with the Piedmont Post.

articles.text: More than 20 students from Piedmont High School and Piedmont Middle School spent the Saturday before Thanksgiving volunteering at CityTeam Oakland. They helped prepare and serve a community meal for people experiencing homelessness. The event, organized annually through Piedmont Community Church, is a long-standing tradition that brings local families CityTeam Oakland provides meals, groceries and shelter services throughout the year. The Saturday meal is one of its regular community gatherings and offers guests a warm place to share food. Students and parent volunteers prepared pot roast, baked ziti, vegetables and apple crisp. Wearing white shirts and black pants, students greeted guests, served meals and cleared tables. Nearly two hundred meals were served, and extra portions were packaged for the next day. “These students spent countless hours planning, preparing and serving a nutritious meal at CityTeam Oakland for those experiencing homelessness. Seeing young people lead with such humility, strength and love gives me immense hope for the world they are shaping,” said Kerry Perschitte of Piedmont Community Church. Her comments matched the atmosphere in the dining room, where students stayed busy throughout the evening and guests expressed appreciation for the meal and the volunteers. Students said meeting guests was a meaningful part of the evening. articles.text: When it comes to building a child’s vocabulary, parents often imagine flashcards, worksheets, or structured lessons. While these tools have their place, the most powerful vocabulary lessons often happen naturally—during daily routines and ordinary moments at home. As a speech-language pathologist, I’ve seen how simple, everyday activities can provide rich opportunities for language growth and comprehension, helping children develop the words they need to communicate effectively. Everyday Conversations Matter Vocabulary grows when children are exposed to new words in meaningful contexts. Mealtime, cooking, laundry, or grocery shopping can all become language lessons. Describing what’s happening, labeling objects, and talking about actions encourages children to connect words with real experiences. For example, asking a child to help “measure the flour” or “fold the towels” introduces verbs and nouns in a practical context. Ask Questions That Invite Thinking Instead of yes/no questions, try open-ended prompts that encourage children to explain, predict, or compare. Questions like “Why do you think the cake needs to bake?” or “Which shirt should we wear today and why?” encourage children to articulate ideas, use descriptive language, and practice reasoning. This not only expands vocabulary but also strengthens critical thinking skills. Read Together—Interactively Reading remains one of the best ways to grow vocabulary. Make it interactive: pause to discuss new words, ask your child to predict what will happen next, or connect the story to real-life experiences. Picture books, nonfiction texts, or even comic strips can all introduce new concepts and language in fun, engaging ways. Use Play and Hands-On Activities Play is a natural way to build language. Pretend play, building blocks, art projects, or even outdoor exploration offer opportunities to describe actions, colors, shapes, and materials. Encourage children to narrate what they are doing or explain their choices. This not only reinforces vocabulary but also strengthens narrative skills—an important foundation for reading comprehension. Model Rich Language Yourself Children learn by imitation. Use descriptive words, varied sentence structures, and expressive language in your own speech. Instead of “Put your shoes on,” try “Can you carefully tie your blue sneakers so they don’t come undone?” Small changes in everyday language expose children to more words naturally, without pressure or drills. Katie Pengilly is a Speech and Language Pathologist, and the owner of SPEECH Inc., a pediatric private practice specializing in speech, language, reading and writing. articles.text: Photos by Jenni Tsoi Best Piedmont’s girls’ cross country reached State for the first time since 2019. Pictured are Nikita Gorelik (left), Viviane Oesterer, Skylar Best, Leighton Mand, Amalia Gray, Cora Chun, and Cora Brozowski Schrader. Piedmont High’s girls’ cross country team made its way to Woodward Park for the 2025 CIF State Cross Country Championship on Saturday, November 29. With 438 points, the Highlanders finished the day in 18th of 25 schools in the Division 4 category. It marked the first Piedmont’s team qualified for State since 2019, while continuing the school’s 37-year tradition of having at least one athlete qualify for the state championships. “The PHS Varsity girls team culminated their season with a trip to the state meet, the first since 2019. The girls ran for each other all season and they ran as a pack – that was their strength,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach.. Leading the charge for the Highlanders was junior Leighton Mand, who placed 96th in a field of 205 runners with a time of 19:52.3 on the 5,000-meter course. Mand finished as Piedmont’s top runner in eight meets this season, including the De La Salle Nike Invitational on September 20, the WACC Championship on November 8, and the North Coast Section Championship on November 22. “It’s not easy to get to the State meet,” Zirkelbach said. “There are so many obstacles to endure, from the long season which can result in fatigue or injuries.” Behind Mand was senior Skylar Best in 112th, with a time of 20:13.8. It marked her second CIF State appearance after last competing at State as a freshman in 2022. “It’s great to bookend my high school career in this way. It’s so much more meaningful for me to qualify as a team instead of just as an individual. It’s really special,” Best said. Viviane Oesterer was next in for Piedmont, finishing 118th in 20:19.7, while Amalia Gray was behind her 11 spots in 129th in 20:35.2. Rounding out Piedmont’s best five runners was senior Cora Chun, clocking a 20:44.5 to finish 133rd. Chun had to persevere through an early-season injury and came on strong late in the season. “Cora Chun’s return from an early season injury really helped the team, as did the steady performances of the rest of the team,” Zirkelbach said. Looking ahead to next year’s team, the Highlanders could bring back a strong group poised to push for another State berth. Of PHS’ top eight runners on the varsity roster, only Best and Chun are set to graduate. That means lead runners like Mand, Gray, and Oesterer could be back in the fold, while junior Cora Brozowski Schrader, sophomore Nikita Gorelik, and freshman Kelsey Coleman provide considerable talent. “Our third runner, Viviane, and Cora Brozowki Schrader continued to get faster and show their racing grit. That’s something that I look forward to using as the foundation for next year’s team,” Zirkelbach said. Skylar Best ran the final race of her Piedmont cross country career. She was a four-year starter and last qualified for State as an individual in 2022. Leighton Mand led the way for Piedmont, placing 96th of 205 runners.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team isn’t sneaking up on anyone this year. Matter of fact, there’s now a target on their backs. The Highlanders return to Binks Rawlings Gym for the 2025-26 season after finishing last year with a 25-6 record. Piedmont reached the North Coast Section Open Division as the No. 5 seed and fought their way to the Division 1 CIF State Regional Semifinals as the No. 8 seed. They did all that with a roster that featured three freshmen, Jenelle Solis, Andrea Martin, and Savannah Dennig, and one sophomore Taylor White. Now with an added year of experience, coach Bryan Gardere knows that everyone in the basketball community has their eyes on Piedmont. “Our schedule is tougher and there’s no sneaking up on anybody. We’re going to get the best of the teams we’re going against. No one truly knows your expectations your freshman year, but now can you match those expectations? Our whole thing is we’re trying to compete and work hard every day, you have to hold that bar really high,” Gardere said. Martin, Solis, Dennig and White burst onto the scene last year. Martin was the first freshman to be named honorable mention for Athlete of the Year by the Post. “Andrea is a big guard, but she can play one through five. We expect her to do a little bit of everything. We’re excited for her and think she can handle all those responsibilities,” Gardere said. Solis was the Post’s Freshman of the Year, showing her quality and savvy as Piedmont’s primary ball handler. She was named the Western Alameda County Conference Player of the Year. “Jenelle is looking to build off her MVP year. She’s a big part of what we do. We really leaned on her to be the primary ball handler. Her shooting and finishing has gotten even better during the offseason,” Gardere said. Dennig was honorable mention for Freshman of the Year and very much embodied the heart and soul of the team. She represents one of the most gritty and selfless players on the court, giving her all on every loose ball and rebound. “Savannah is a crowd favorite because of the way she plays Staff Photos Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team is back after reaching last year’s NCS Open Division and the CIF State Division 1 tournament. with a reckless abandon. She’s heart and soul, energy, and has maybe taken the biggest leap with her development. At the alumni game, she made six 3-pointers. She’s been working tirelessly on her game,” Gardere said. White was our honorable mention for Sophomore of the Year after proving to be vital in each phase of the game. “Taylor is going to play a big role on both sides [offense and defense]. Taylor is going to be someone we’ll lean on to take care of the ball and she usually defends team’s better players. We expect her to continue to play that role and to be aggressive offensively as well,” Gardere said. Piedmont faces the task of replacing key scorer Briana Webb, who is starting her basketball career at Fresno State. Shakila Zuberi was Class of 2025 graduate who made an impact with her leadership on defense. With that, Saniyah Johnson makes the jump to the starting lineup. “We lose those two seniors, but all of our returners were contributors in some shape. Saniyah Johnson has come into her own and is playing some good basketball right now. She’s our only senior,” Gardere said. There’s also a freshman poised to make an impact, Alexa Ba, the daughter of assistant coach Mbissane Ba. Although Alexa is new to the school, she isn’t exactly new to the team, having been on the bench and attending practice over the last few years. Gardere calls her a “bonafide” college prospect. “Alexa is already one of our better finishers and shooters. It’ll take her a year or two, but she can get rebounds and draw fouls. She is definitely going to be one of our key players,” Gardere said. PHS gets its season started on Thursday, December 11 with its annual Paris Twins Classic going through Saturday, December 13. They are set to take on Oakland High on Thursday at 5:30 p.m. in the Binks Rawlings Gym. Jenelle Solis was the Post’s Freshman of the Year in 2025. Andrea Martin was the Post’s honorable mention pick for Athlete of the Year in 2025, becoming the first freshman to be named to our top end-of-year award.

articles.text: Soccer team promoted to National Premier League The Piedmont Soccer Club (PSC) 2014 Girls Purple capped off a landmark season with a 2–0 win over Revolution FC, closing Fall 2025 with both strong results and a place in club history. The team finished second in Pre-National Premier League and, in the process, became the first team in Piedmont Soccer Club history to compete at the NPL 1 level — the highest statewide competitive tier for their age group. For a team that has focused on steady development over several years, the achievement represents a significant milestone. The group’s upward trajectory began last year, when they captured the Fall League Gold title, earning advancement into the East Bay Premier bracket. articles.text: The San Francisco Symphony will perform George Frideric Handel’s Messiah, a musical meditation on Christ’s birth, life, and resurrection, this Friday, December 5 and Saturday, December 6. Conductor Jane Glover leads the symphony and chorus in this classic holiday favorite. Glover is a fellow of the Royal College of Music and was the artistic director of opera at the Royal Academy of Music between 2009 and 2016. In December 2013, she became the third woman ever to conduct at the Metropolitan Opera of New York, leading Mozart’s The Magic Flute. Performances include Susanna Phillips as soprano, Jennifer Johnson Cano as mezzo-soprano, Josh Lovell as tenor, and Will Liverman as baritone. Davies Symphony Hall will be decked out for the holidays during these performances, filled with lit evergreen trees, wreaths and garlands. The hall’s lobby bar will feature festive winter cocktails, including a Gingerbread Old Fashioned, limited-time sparkling wine and holiday-themed desserts throughout December. The Friday and Saturday performances both begin at 7:30 p.m. A preconcert talk by San Francisco Symphony’s resident lecturer Laura Stanfield Prichard will be presented onstage at 6:30 p.m. before both performances. The preconcert talk is free to all ticketholders. Tickets are on sale now. Visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2025-26/ H ANDEL-MESSIAH or call the box office at (415) 864-6000 to purchase tickets. Jennifer Johnson Cano

articles.text: Cast of Sunday in the Park with George Shotgun Players closes out its 2025 season with a new production of Sunday in the Park with George, the Pulitzer Prize–winning musical by Stephen Sondheim and James Lapine, showing now through December 30 at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley. articles.text: Alejandro Cartagena The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) is exhibiting Alejandro Cartagena: Ground Rules now through April 2026, marking the first retrospective of the acclaimed photographer’s career. The exhibition features two decades of Cartagena’s work and more than 20 major projects exploring themes of urban development, migration, and environmental change in Mexico. Known for his inventive use of landscape photography and portraiture, Cartagena employs the camera as a tool for examining social and ecological shifts in contemporary life. Born in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, in 1977, Cartagena has lived and worked in Monterrey, Mexico, since his youth. His photographs have been featured in more than 50 solo and group exhibitions worldwide, including the Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona in Spain and the Fondation Cartier pour l’Art Contemporain in Paris. His work is held in the permanent collections of institutions such as the J. Paul Getty Museum, the Museum of Fine Arts in Houston, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, and the Museum of Contemporary Photography in Chicago. Cartagena’s early projects, including Identidad Nuevo León (2005) and Espacios Habitables (2004–05), reflect on belonging and identity, while later series such as Between Borders (2009– 10), Americanos (2012–14), and Without Walls (2017) explored U.S.-Mexico relations and gained him international recognition. Works like Suburbia Mexicana (2005–10) and Carpoolers (2011– 12) examine the effects of rapid suburban growth, highlighting economic disparities and environmental transformation. In recent years, Cartagena has expanded his practice to include collage, video, and AI-generated imagery, as seen in Photo Structures (2018–19) and his latest video series, We Are Things (2025). “Photography changed our world two centuries ago; the way we see it, and the way we think about it has never been the same since we started using it,” Cartagena said in a press release. “I want to be part of that history of how the medium transformed our understanding of social, political and environmental issues through images.” SFMOMA Director Christopher Bedford said Cartagena’s photographs “open up broad conversations that transcend geography.” “Cartagena’s work invites reflection and probing questions that serve to complicate our understanding of important social and environmental topics. I believe this exhibition will resonate deeply with our audiences,” he added. The exhibition will be on view through April 19, 2026. Visit sfmoma.org or call (415) 357- 4000 for more information.

articles.text: Good Fire: Tending Native Lands and Students on Strike on view now The Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) is inviting all East Bay residents to take advantage of its monthly “First Sundays,” a regular day of increased access and community connection. This Sunday, December 7, and every first Sunday of the month, general admission to OMCA’s galleries of California art, history, and natural sciences is free. “First Sundays” run from 11:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., giving ample time to explore exhibits, relax in the newly updated garden, or browse locally-made goods at the museum shop. Whether you’re curious about California’s history, local art, or natural science, “First Sundays” at OMCA offer a great chance to engage with Oakland and the local community’s culture and to bring friends, family, or neighbors along for a relaxed Sunday outing. Visitors are encouraged to reserve tickets online in advance to secure a preferred entry time and reduce wait times. While general admission is free, time slots can fill up on busy days. For those interested in special exhibitions in OMCA’s Great Hall, discounted tickets are offered on First Sundays. Special exhibitions open now include Good Fire: Tending Native Lands and Students on Strike. OMCA’s newest exhibition, Good Fire: Tending Native Lands explores cultural and historical significance of Northern California’s native communities’ use of fire and presents the significance of intentional fire use by local tribes whose practices predate state and federal fire management systems. Students on Strike highlights the 1968 student-led strike at San Francisco State University (SFSU) and other noteworthy movements that established the nation’s first Black Studies Department and first College of Ethnic Studies at the university. Visit https://museumca.org/ to learn more. OMCA offers free admission every first Sunday of the month.

articles.text: The World’s Fair in Paris in 1889 opened the European world to the rest of the world. The Eiffel Tower is the only example that physically remains of that extraordinary fair. But the world changed in many ways. The exhibitions included the cultures of diverse peoples and the people themselves. The souvenirs of that fair were almost as diverse as the exhibitions. Many important European composers attended in 1889. Is it a coincidence that their music changed… literally overnight? They became aware of the beauties beyond their borders. Far flung European empires became all the more encompassing. French composer Maurice Ravel is an excellent example of this transformation. This was the case, exemplified by the first piece on the program on Sunday afternoon in Piedmont’s Center for the Arts. Ravel was inspired by the “exotic” aspect of the Orient. (We use the word Asia now instead of Orient.) His music added new flavors in music which resonated with his listeners. The music allowed the listeners’ imagination to take flight. The gas-filled dirigibles were around, but airplanes were a generation away. The important name of the time was Nadar. The Wright Brothers had to wait. Ravel offered his musical perspective. Soprano Jennifer Lien explained her standpoint from a different perspective. Her’s is an authentically Asian one. Some might think that the difference of opinion was a combat instead of a basic conundrum. Fortunately, music forces us to think in a wider perspective. Ravel was the only historical composer on Sunday’s program. What came next were compositions by Melissa Dunphy, Kamala Sankaram, and Justine F. Chen. All of these composers are contemporary, and the music was co-commissioned by soprano Jennifer Lien. The whole concert was like going to an art exhibition. Each artist sees things from an original and unique perspective. articles.text: A scene brom Disney’s Bolt Bolt is a lively, family-friendly Disney adventure that young viewers will happily settle into. The story opens with sevenyear-old Penny, voiced by Miley Cyrus, who adopts a White Swiss Shepherd puppy she names Bolt, played by John Travolta. Five years later, the two are stars of a hit action TV series, battling the schemes of the villainous Dr. Calico. To keep Bolt’s performance sharp, the show’s director works hard to convince him that his superpowers — including his trademark “super bark” — are real. Penny is uneasy with the ruse, knowing Bolt can never leave the set without the truth becoming clear. During one cliffhanger episode, Penny’s character is kidnapped. Bolt believes the danger is real, escapes the studio, and accidentally ends up inside a packing crate of peanuts. Knocked unconscious and shipped across the country, he lands in New York City. Lost and confused, Bolt meets Mittens, a wary, streetwise cat voiced by Susie Essman, and insists they must return to Hollywood to rescue Penny. Back at the studio, producers quickly replace Bolt with another White Swiss Shepherd so the show can go on, despite Penny’s reluctance. Meanwhile, Bolt and Mittens begin an eventful cross-country journey. In Ohio, they tangle with animal control and pick up an unlikely ally: Rhino, an exuberant hamster and Bolt super-fan, voiced by Mark Walton. The trio presses on toward California, forging an unexpected bond along the way. Once they reach Hollywood, one final crisis strikes on the studio lot. But this is Disney, and the film brings things home with a warm, satisfying ending. Bolt and Penny are reunited, and Penny adopts both Mittens and Rhino, giving the trio a real home at last. Bolt is earnest, energetic, and sweet-natured — a gentle reminder that sometimes the greatest superpower is loyalty. Bolt. Directed by Chris Williams and Byron Howard. Walt Disney Animation. Voiced by John Travolta, Miley Cyrus, Susie Essman. Genre adventure. Duration 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG. Released 2016. Streaming on Disney+, Fandango, Apple, Prime. With story hour concluded, Matt was ready to lead the group on the official Piedmont Turkey Trot 5K course. Before setting out, he shared a few statistics. According to Google, in 2024 approximately 1.1 million people participated in Thanksgiving Turkey Trot races across the United States, with 936 races held nationwide. Participation was up 21 percent from the previous year, and these events collectively raised more than $3.6 million for charities, making Thanksgiving the biggest running day of the year. In one peak year, participation topped 3,100, but that size was eventually deemed unsafe and the number of runners was capped. The Tibetans call her Chomolungma (Goddess Mother of the World). On April 1, 2019 Piedmont’s Bill Baringer embarked on an eightweek dance with the goddess in cold weather and long days. His trip started in Kathmandu, Nepal, elevation 4,593 ft., where the peril ramped up immediately with a flight to the most dangerous airport in the world, Lukla, at 9,330 ft. The runway at Lukla is very short and not level; it is on an incline. “Planes don’t glide into it, they kind of just smack into it, like a fly on a wall,” recalled Baringer. There were problems with the runway at the time, so he and his climbing group took helicopters, a little more expensive, but a lot safer. Bill chose the company “Climbing The Seven Summits,” owned by legendary mountain guide Mike Hamill, and found himself part of a group of 24 climbers. This would be a twomonth program in Nepal to give the group the best chance of acclimatizing, and to account for weather setbacks, which turned out to be very much needed. After having climbed the highest peak on five other continents, he prepared for Everest with months of training at home with a heavy backpack. Each climber was allowed to bring two 50-pound duffel bags, one to be taken directly to Everest base camp and the other carried to sleeping accommodations each evening by porters. Bill thought each porter was going to carry one 50 lb. bag, but they tied two bags together and went up the mountain. Bill was amazed at their strength and endurance. ”I’m not going anywhere with 100 pounds on my back. They took amazing loads,” he said of the porters. Bill’s journey commenced through the Khumbu Valley along the glacier melt of the Dudh Kosi River. On April 4 the trek from Phakding to Namche Bazaar required a significant elevation change of 2,727’ up the steep Namche Hill. Namche Bazaar had upgraded and expanded significantly since Bill’s paragliding trip to the region with his wife in 1995. articles.text: In the summer of 2010, Stephen Main, Director of Music at Piedmont Community Church, had the wonderful idea of pulling the special Christmas music with choir and five instruments out of a Sunday service and presenting it in the evening. First, it would not be limited to twenty minutes; it could run a full hour and include a full symphony orchestra. Second, it would recognize that many people in Piedmont and surrounding communities love beautiful Christmas music standing on its own. Third, the concert could be followed by a festive holiday reception. And so the Overture to Christmas tradition was born. Every year, Stephen conducts a concert with full orchestra, 45 voice choir and soloists. Each one has a unique theme related to the Christmas story. These have included angels, shepherds, the animals around the manger, Mary, Joseph, love, instruments used in Christmas music and more. This year, Stephen has chosen the theme of Christmas – Through the Eyes of a Child. Until the second half of the 19th century children were not included in the religious observation. As childhood became viewed as a separate life stage, the privileged connection between innocent children and God coming to earth as a helpless baby grew. The pieces included in this year’s concert explore this idea and range from medieval to contemporary. The audience is invited to sing four traditional carols with the orchestra, which is great fun. Following the concert join us for a joyful reception. Mingle with your neighbors and the musicians. Enjoy a buffet of sweets and savories, wine, coffee, punch and lots of good fellowship.
